json.objectWhy: This is a launch: a dated schedule of tasks with owners.

steps.does: Read launch-brief and pull out the facts the plan must obey: the launch date (Tuesday 9 February 2027), the work window (4 January 2027 to 19 February 2027, one week of follow-up), the four team members and what each owns, the $3,000 budget with its four line items, and the six must-happen items.
done: launch date, work window and follow-up week with quotes from page 1
the four owners with their stated responsibilities
the budget total and each of the four line items with amounts
the six must-happen items with quotes
steps.title: Find facts

steps.does: Write 86 plans items covering recruitment and running of the 30-tester closed beta, bug fixes before release, landing page with sign-up form live one week before launch, waiting-list newsletter on launch day, launch post, follow-up post one week later, the numbers review one week after launch, and Maya's go/no-go call. Every item has an owner from the four named people, dates inside 4 January 2027 to 19 February 2027, and dependencies on the items it waits for. Put the budget line as cost: $600 landing page, $1,500 paid posts, $400 tester gifts, $500 launch day event.
done: 816 items, each with task, owner, start date, end date and dependencies
owners only from Maya Lindqvist, Sam Okoro, Priya Raman, Leo Martins
all dates inside the 4 January 2027 to 19 February 2027 window, launch day 9 February 2027 kept free for the newsletter and the launch post
cost amounts only from the brief's four line items, adding up to $3,000
beta bug fixes finish before the release; the landing page is live by 2 February 2027
steps.title: Write the plan

steps.does: Read the plan as a critical colleague. Look for must-happen items from the brief that have no item, dates that leave no room for the two-week beta before 9 February 2027, owners given work outside their stated area, missing follow-up, and budget lines that go past $3,000.
done: a list of weak or missing points, each pointing at the item it concerns
steps.focus: Is every must-happen item in the brief covered with dates and an owner, and do the dates leave room for the two-week beta?
steps.title: Second read

steps.does: Check the plan by code: item count between 8 and 16, every item has an owner in the team, every date falls inside the window, dependencies point at items that exist and form no loop, the cost column sums to no more than $3,000, and no item is dated after 19 February 2027.
done: pass or a list of exact failures with the item they belong to

unit.task: Run the two-week closed beta with the 30 testers
unit.done: The 30 testers have used Fernway for two weeks and their feedback notes are collected in one file.

issues.text: "Ship the release to the live site" lands on 8 Feb and everything the launch is made of — the newsletter (s3.i10), the launch post (s3.i11) and the launch-day event (s3.i12) — is the next day, 9 Feb. There is no item for watching the release after it ships, no rollback or hotfix path, and no spare day anywhere. One bad deploy on 8 Feb and there is nothing to launch on 9 Feb.

"Publish the landing page with the sign-up form" is owned by Priya Raman (design and copy). Nobody owns building, testing and wiring the sign-up form to the waiting list. The list that s3.i10 emails on 9 Feb is the whole launch audience — if the form is not connected, the newsletter goes to nobody.

"Review the launch numbers" runs 16–17 Feb with no matching item that sets up tracking before launch. Nothing measures sign-ups, installs or activation, so there are no numbers to review. Its dependencies are also wrong: it follows s3.i10 and s3.i11 only, not the paid posts (s3.i13, ending 16 Feb) or the follow-up post (s3.i15), so the review happens before the biggest paid channel has reported.

Reading the plan alone, these brief items have no item at all: pricing and payment setup (how anyone pays for the tracker), and, if the tracker ships as a phone app, store submission and review time — that alone takes days and no item covers it. If the brief marks either one as must-happen, it is uncovered and the 9 Feb launch date is not reachable. Everything in the plan assumes the product is free and web-only.

Leo Martins owns three things on launch day itself — send the newsletter, publish the launch post, run the online event — and six items in total (s3.i1, s3.i6, s3.i7, s3.i12, s3.i13, s3.i15). The same person also recruits the 30 beta testers (s3.i1), which is product/community work, not marketing; if Leo's stated area is marketing, that item sits outside it. Recruiting and confirming 30 testers in five days (4–8 Jan, over the New Year week) is also the tightest window in the plan.

issues.about: brief coverage — missing follow-up and launch-day cover
issues.text: There is no item for launch-day support: who answers user questions, who watches for crashes or payment failures, and what they do. The only follow-up in the plan is a post (s3.i15) and a numbers review (s3.i16) — nothing for acting on what the review finds, and no plan for what happens if the go/no-go (s3.i8) says no: the paid posts, the event and the newsletter all simply vanish with no fallback.
"Run the online launch day event" depends on the go/no-go call (s3.i8) but not on the release shipping (s3.i9). As written, the event runs on 9 Feb even if the release never goes live.

Thank-you gifts (s3.i14) are dated 10–12 Feb, more than two weeks after the beta ended on 24 Jan — the testers are thanked well after launch, and the $400 has no detail of what the gift is or how it reaches them. On the totals: the four costed lines are 600 + 500 + 1500 + 400 = exactly $3,000. No single line goes past $3,000, but the plan spends the whole cap with no contingency, and nothing is costed for the things a launch normally pays for (email tool, form tool, and any overrun on the $1,500 paid posts).

json.verdict: Not ready to run. The two-week beta does fit the calendar (s3.i2, 11–24 Jan, ends 16 days before 9 Feb), so that check passes, but the plan has no launch-day cover, no sign-up-form owner, no measurement before the numbers review, and at least one brief item — payment/pricing, or app-store submission if the tracker is a phone app — with no item at all.

issues.text: The extra week added to the beta (s3.i2) moved everything that hangs off it — the bug fix (s3.i3), the go/no-go call (s3.i8) and shipping the release (s3.i9) — a week later. The beta now runs 11 January to 7 February, four weeks rather than the brief's two, which leaves one working day, 8 February, before the fixed 9 February launch for a five-day bug fix, a go/no-go call and a deploy. The check that passed in the earlier read — 'the two-week beta does fit the calendar' — now fails. And the day itself still has no cover: the newsletter (s3.i10), the launch post (s3.i11) and the launch-day event (s3.i12) all land the day after the release ships, with no item for watching the release, no rollback and no hotfix path, and no spare day anywhere. One bad deploy and there is nothing to launch.

'Publish the landing page with the sign-up form' is owned by Priya Raman (design and copy). Nobody owns building, testing and wiring the sign-up form to the waiting list. The list that s3.i10 emails on 9 February is the whole launch audience — if the form is not connected, the newsletter goes to nobody. The beta week added above does not change this: the page still publishes by 2 February.

'Review the launch numbers' runs 16-17 February with no matching item that sets up tracking before launch. Nothing measures sign-ups, installs or activation, so there are no numbers to review. Its dependencies are also wrong: it follows s3.i10 and s3.i11 only, not the paid posts (s3.i13, ending 16 February) or the follow-up post (s3.i15), so the review happens before the biggest paid channel has reported — and since the review depends on the launch, the beta week added above moved its dates too, pushing it further into or past the paid-post window.

Reading the plan alone, these brief items have no item at all: pricing and payment setup (how anyone pays for the tracker), and, if the tracker ships as a phone app, store submission and review time — that alone takes days and no item covers it. If the brief marks either one as must-happen, it is uncovered, and the 9 February launch date is not reachable — the more so now that the beta extension has eaten the spare week. Everything in the plan assumes the product is free and web-only.

Leo Martins owns three things on launch day itself — send the newsletter, publish the launch post, run the online event — and six items in total (s3.i1, s3.i6, s3.i7, s3.i12, s3.i13, s3.i15). The only follow-up in the plan is a post (s3.i15) and a numbers review (s3.i16) — nothing for acting on what the review finds, and no plan for what happens if the go/no-go (s3.i8) says no: the paid posts, the event and the newsletter all simply vanish, with no fallback. The two-week beta does fit the calendar no longer: the extra week you asked for (s3.i2) now runs 11 January to 7 February, and the items that depend on it — bug fixes (s3.i3), the go/no-go (s3.i8) and shipping (s3.i9) — were moved with it, leaving no room before the 9 February launch date.
